newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore Lee's place in history scrutinised.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore Lee's place in history scrutinised.

text.p: Two years before stepping down as prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew said he would rise from his grave if he felt Singapore was in danger of hitting the rocks.

"Those who believe that when I have left the government as prime minister, that I've gone into permanent retirement, really should have their heads examined," he said in a speech to the nation in 1988.
"And even from my sick bed, even if you are going to lower me into the grave and I feel something is going wrong, I'll get up."

Now, seven years after Lee assumed the role of elder statesman as Senior Minister, some analysts are wondering whether his continued presence in domestic and foreign affairs is an asset or a liability.
In March last year, after a second heart treatment, the 73-year-old Lee admitted it was time to slow down, "to move to a slightly easier pace...accepting the limitations of age".

But political analysts said Lee was still passionate in his belief that Singapore's national interests must always come first and nothing, internally or externally, should subvert the prosperity he helped build in his 31 years as leader.
A Singapore politican said this belief was what motivated Lee to speak his mind on whatever he considered important.

"The man has encouraged the U.S. to engage China for years," said the ruling party backbencher. "Now that America has decided to engage China...that can have a positive effect on the security and development in Asia-Pacific."
OUTSPOKENNESS MAY RILE NEIGHBOURS

But regional analysts said Lee's outspokenness could rile neighbours, not least Malaysia, which he enraged with a remark in March that its southern state of Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Lee made the remark in an affidavit in pursuit of a libel suit against opposition Singapore politican Tang Liang Hong, who fled to Johor.
Malaysia demanded a retraction. The youth wing of its ruling party insulted Lee and this angered many Singaporeans.

Lee apologised twice for the remark, which Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said was "offside", and applied to get it removed from court records. Kuala Lumpur accepted the apology but said it would take time to for the wound to heal.

The row appeared to have escalated last week when several Malaysian ministers were quoted as saying a cabinet meeting, held while Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad was away in Japan, had decided to freeze new bilateral dealings with Singapore.

Mahathir said while Lee's remarks still rankled Malaysians, the issue was not a major problem. The cabinet clarified that only some tourism, cultural and sporting links had been suspended, not commercial and economic ties.
"I think he could have gone out in a blaze of glory in 1990 when he handed over the torch, but he didn't," a Singapore lawyer said of Lee.
The lawyer, who asked not to be identified, said Lee should move away from active, partisan politics. "He can be a Helmut Schmidt, Giscard d'Estaing...or Henry Kissinger."

"Lee Kuan Yew represents one of very few politicians able to articulate their views but these comments about Asia sometimes seemed ill judged," said Takashi Inoguchi, senior vice-rector at the United Nations University in Tokyo.
A TEST OF STATESMANSHIP
"Most likely it's a case of as his age goes up it becomes easier to say his feelings without balance and measure."
Inoguchi said being provocative was often a good thing, "but to worsen relations with a close neighbour is not the behaviour of a good statesman".
Nelson Navarro, columnist with the Manila Standard newspaper said Lee had become "politically incorrect" and the episode with Malaysia could lessen his profile.
But other analysts said Lee had been very careful in ensuring a smooth transition and did not seek a high profile.
Raj K. Vasil, an expert in Singapore politics at New Zealand's University of Victoria, said Lee had been very fair to the second generation leadership even when he was in power.
"Lee told Goh and others it was only fair that no policy should be pursued which they did not agree with, as Lee's generation would not face the consequences."
Once Goh took over, Lee did not interfere in decision making or use his position to influence decisions, Vasil said.
But if Lee disagreed with a policy, he would make it a point to warn Goh "he might comment about it in public sometimes...Goh told me he had no problems with that," Vasil said.
Vasil said Lee, in his role as tutor, made sure his successors remembered what happened during the formation of the Malaysian federation and Singapore's separation from it.
"Lee talks with them about the need to retain the sensitivities and historical perspective," Vasil said.
HISTORICAL BAGGAGE OF OLDER GENERATIONS

But other analysts noted an irony here because these very "sensitivities", over an era that saw Singapore separating from Malaysia after a brief marriage between 1963 and 1965, often hampered efforts to elevate relations to a new level.

Singapore's Straits Times said in an editorial the row over Lee's remark showed the "historical baggage" from that era that Mahathir and Malaysians of his generation carry. "Not that Mr Lee and older Singaporeans are free of it either," it said.
"They cannot help but look at each other through prisms, which their younger compatriots will find somewhat outdated."

But the backbencher said Lee was as agile as ever, mentally and physically, and his position in Singapore and in history has never been threatened, he said. "It's not being threatened now even by this episode (with Malaysia)."
